segments.english: Abraham set out from there for the land of the Negev, and he lived between Kadesh and Shur, and he sojourned in Gerar.
segments.literal: and-journeyed from-there Abraham to-land the-Negev and-dwelt between Kadesh and-between Shur and-sojourned in-Gerar

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of נָסַע: 'pull out (the tent pegs), set out'; the departure from a place.
The text does not name the place 'there'; 18:1 places Abraham at Mamre.
The directional he (אַרְצָה) on a construct: 'to the land of'. 'Land' here is a region (2.b): the Negev.
wayyiqtol of יָשַׁב: 'dwell, have one's abode'.
The lexicon's first sense: the Kadesh in the south of Judah.
wayyiqtol of גּוּר: to live as a resident without owning land.

phrases.literal: and-set-out from-there Abraham: the verb leads the clause in Hebrew; the subject follows it

phrases.english: for the land of the Negev
phrases.literal: to-land the-Negev: the directional he gives 'to'
and-between Shur: Hebrew repeats the preposition before the second place; English does not

grammar: Three wayyiqtol verbs (וַיִּסַּע, וַיֵּשֶׁב, וַיָּגָר) carry the narrative in sequence: a move, a stay, and a longer residence.
The repeated preposition in בֵּין־קָדֵשׁ וּבֵין שׁוּר gives two separate points, with Kadesh and Shur as the ends of the place where Abraham dwelt.
The accents divide the verse at the etnaḥta on שׁ֑וּר, so the first half gives the journey and the stay and the second gives the residence in Gerar.
The place-names carry no article: קָדֵשׁ, שׁוּר and גְּרָר are proper names; the lexicon's first sense for קָדֵשׁ is the Kadesh of the south.
segments.note: The narrative of 20:1 moves without comment on the reason for the journey; the commentators supply motives (see commentary), which are not in the English.

commentary.summary: Radak: the Negev is the southern part of the land of Israel, since the inheritance of Judah lay to the south. The English keeps 'the land of the Negev' as a part of the land.

Radak takes 'from there' as the oaks of Mamre, where Abraham lived, and suggests he went into the land of the Philistines, which is within the land God gave him. The English keeps 'from there' and does not name the place.

Radak: 'dwelt' and 'sojourned' are one matter restated in a doubled clause; Abraham may first have dwelt by the well of Lahai, between Kadesh and Shur, and then come to Gerar. The English keeps the two verbs apart as the Hebrew does.
Sforno reads Kadesh and Shur as two great cities, and says Abraham settled between them to call on the name of the LORD, El Olam. The English takes both as places and adds nothing about cities.
Targum Onkelos renders Kadesh as Rekem and Shur as Hagra, and keeps Gerar. The English keeps the Hebrew names, since those identifications are not settled.

Rashi gives a motive for leaving: the towns were ruined and travellers stopped, and Abraham moved away because of the bad name Lot had after his deeds with his daughters. This is a reason for the move, not the sense of the words.

context: The Negev: the dry south country, south of the hill country of Judah around Beersheba. The Hebrew word also means 'south'.

Kadesh and Shur: 16:14 places a well 'between Kadesh and Bered'; 25:18 puts Shur 'before Egypt', so it lay on the south-western edge of the land toward Egypt (16:7 speaks of 'the road to Shur'). Kadesh here is not the northern Kadesh of the lexicon's sense 2.
Gerar: a town of the south-west, at the edge of the Negev. Its exact site is disputed.

segments.english: Abraham said of Sarah his wife, "She is my sister." Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took Sarah.
segments.literal: and-said Abraham to Sarah his-wife my-sister she and-sent Abimelech king of-Gerar and-took (object) Sarah

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of אָמַר: the narrative verb that introduces the speech.
אֶל with a person, read by Ibn Ezra as על, 'about, concerning'.
construct of אִשָּׁה with the 3ms suffix.
construct of אָחוֹת with the 1cs suffix.
The pronoun is feminine, agreeing with Sarah; the statement has no verb.
wayyiqtol of שָׁלַח.
The lexicon's first sense: the king of Gerar.
wayyiqtol of לָקַח. What the taking means is developed in 20:3.
The object marker has no English counterpart.

phrases.literal: concerning Sarah his-wife: Ibn Ezra's 'like על'
my-sister she: the subject follows the predicate; no copula in Hebrew
and-sent Abimelech king of-Gerar: the subject is placed before the verb in English

grammar: Three wayyiqtol verbs (וַיֹּאמֶר, וַיִּשְׁלַח, וַיִּקַּח) carry the narrative. Abraham's words are set without quotation marks in the Hebrew.
The statement אֲחֹתִי הִוא has no verb: the feminine pronoun agrees with Sarah, and the English supplies 'is'.
The etnaḥta on הִ֑וא ends Abraham's words, and the revia on וַיִּשְׁלַ֗ח begins the report of the king's act.
The object marker אֶת before שָׂרָה has no English counterpart, so it is given as '-' in the phrase.
segments.note: The preposition אֶל before a person is read by Ibn Ezra as 'concerning', like על, and the English takes that reading. The name of Sarah's relation is Abraham's word; the English keeps the statement in the form the Hebrew gives it.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: אל here means על, 'about, concerning', as in 1 Samuel 1:27 'concerning this boy' (אֶל הַנַּעַר הַזֶּה). So Abraham said of Sarah his wife that she was his sister.
Rashi: אל means על here, as in the two parallel uses in 1 Samuel 4 (the taking of the ark and the death of her father-in-law). The English agrees.

Rashi on 'and Abraham said': he did not ask her leave, and spoke against her will and not for her good, since she had already been taken into Pharaoh's house. The English does not say whether she consented.
Radak: אֶל here is 'for the sake of' Sarah his wife; he said it to those who asked him about her.

Radak: אֶל stands for עַל, as in 1 Samuel 17:49 and Ezekiel 18:6. He said this on coming to Gerar, because he judged the people there wicked, as his own words in 20:11 show ('there is no fear of God in this place'); so too Isaac in Gerar. How he could give up his wife without standing the test of his own death was explained earlier, with Pharaoh. Sarah's beauty at ninety: she had returned to youth and to the way of women so that she might conceive.
Ramban: this was not as in Egypt. The king of Gerar was honest and upright, and his men were good; Abraham suspected them without cause and said to all, 'She is my sister.'
Radak on 'and sent': after hearing of her beauty, the king had her brought and took her as his wife. The English 'took' keeps the verb open.
Targum Onkelos renders the phrase as 'concerning Sarah his wife', taking the preposition as 'about'. The English agrees.

apparatus: אֲחֹתִי הִוא (20:2.7): the consonants are הוא (the form of 'he'), vocalised and read as the feminine הִיא (the Pentateuch's standing qere). The English follows the qere, 'she'.
context: Abimelech: the name is usually read as 'my father is king' (אָבִי מֶלֶךְ). Whether it names one king or is a dynastic title is disputed; Psalm 34's superscription gives the name to the king whom 1 Samuel 21 calls Achish.

segments.english: God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him, "You are a dead man because of the woman you have taken, and she is married to a husband."
segments.literal: and-came God to Abimelech in-dream the-night and-said to-him here-you dead on the-woman whom you-took and-she belonging-of a-husband

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of בּוֹא: 'come to' a person.

Plural in form with a singular verb (וַיָּבֹא): the plural of majesty, 'God'. Ibn Ezra explains that the messenger (הַמַּלְאָךְ) came, for Abraham's honour; the plain word is kept in the English and his reading is recorded in the commentary.
The lexicon's second sense: a dream with a message.
The night is the time of the dream.
הִנְּךָ: the demonstrative with the 2ms suffix, presenting the state.
The active participle of מוּת, 'dying' or 'dead'. The English 'a dead man' takes the state of the participle; Sforno reads 'dying' (commentary).
עַל: 'on account of'.
qatal 2ms of לָקַח: the act for which the king is to die.

Feminine construct passive participle of בָּעַל, 'to marry, to be master': 'one possessed by a husband'. The same words stand in Deuteronomy 22:22. The pack parses it as qal; BDB gives 'be married' under Niph. The data is kept.
The lexicon's sense I.2: husband.

phrases.literal: and-came God to Abimelech: אֱלֹהִים is plural in form with a singular verb; Ibn Ezra reads 'the messenger' (note)
in-dream the-night: 'a dream of the night'
here-you dead: the participle gives the state; 'a' is English grammar

phrases.english: and she is married to a husband

grammar: The clause opens with the verb (וַיָּבֹא), then its subject, then the preposition to the king: the English order changes only the placing of the subject.
The etnaḥta on הַלָּ֑יְלָה ends the clause of the dream. The dream is בַּחֲלוֹם הַלָּיְלָה: 'in a dream of the night'.
הִנְּךָ מֵת: a demonstrative with a participle gives the present state, 'you are as one dead'.
The relative clause אֲשֶׁר לָקַחְתָּ refers back to הָאִשָּׁה; the qatal names the act. The last clause, וְהִוא בְּעֻלַת בָּעַל, explains why the taking is a wrong.
segments.note: The subject is אֱלֹהִים, plural in form with a singular verb, as it is of the God of Israel throughout Genesis; the English gives the plain word, 'God'. Ibn Ezra reads that the messenger (הַמַּלְאָךְ) came in the dream, for Abraham's honour; that is his explanation of who came and does not belong in the English line. The contrast he draws with Pharaoh (that Pharaoh and his house were struck with plagues and Abimelech's were not) is also commentary.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: 'And the angel came in the dream to Abimelech, for the honour of Abraham.' He adds that the word 'taking' (לקיחה) is written here as with Pharaoh, but whereas great plagues were brought on Pharaoh and his house, those of Abimelech and his house were not so, 'for he was more righteous than Pharaoh'. The English gives the plain word, 'God'; his reading that a messenger came is kept in the note and the apparatus.

Radak: as said of Laban, a dream of prophecy comes to men of the nations for the honour of the righteous; but Pharaoh was not fit for a dream of prophecy even for their sake, and messengers (שְׁלוּחִין) from God came to him instead. He cites Elihu (Job 33:14–16): God speaks in a dream, a vision of the night. He says a prophetic dream came to Abimelech; he does not speak of an angel.
Radak: she is forbidden to Abimelech because a man must not take another man's wife, which the sons of Noah were also bound by. The English 'belongs to a husband' states the same prohibition.

Radak: the text does not say אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ; the words בְּעֻלַת בָּעַל mean a woman who has been had by her husband, and a betrothed woman is not liable until she has been had by the betrothed. The English 'belongs to a husband' leaves this open.

Sforno: as said of Laban (31:24) and Balaam, no 'he appeared to him', no 'visions of God' and no 'speech' is mentioned, as there is of the patriarchs and the other prophets (Numbers 12:6); the LORD was not seen at all, only a voice came to them. The English says only that God came.
Sforno reads הִנְּךָ מֵת as 'you are going and being consumed by the illness that began in you', so the death is in progress and not yet complete. The English gives the state of a dead man.
Targum Onkelos makes the subject 'a word (מֵימַר) from before the LORD' that came to Abimelech in a dream. The English keeps the Hebrew subject, 'God'.

apparatus: The subject אֱלֹהִים (20:3.2) is plural in form with a singular verb. The English gives 'God'. Ibn Ezra: 'the messenger came in the dream'; Onkelos: 'a word (memra) from before the LORD came'; Sforno: no appearance, only a voice came. In 20:6 the same speaker is הָאֱלֹהִים, 'God'.
context: A dream: the Hebrew חֲלוֹם covers an ordinary dream and a dream carrying a message (lexicon senses 1 and 2); here it carries a message from the divine speaker. In Mesopotamia, Egypt and Canaan a dream was a recognised way for a god to speak to a king.

Marriage: a wife was under her husband's rights in the ancient Near East. בַּעַל is the usual word for a husband and also means 'owner, lord' (lexicon I.1, I.2); בְּעֻלַת בָּעַל is literally 'possessed by an owner'.

Adultery with another man's wife was treated in the law collections of the ancient Near East as a grave offence against the husband, in some, such as the Code of Hammurabi (§129), punished by death. Here the offence is against the husband and God, and the king is told he will die.

segments.english: But Abimelech had not approached her. He said, "My Lord, will you kill a nation, even a righteous one?
segments.literal: and-Abimelech not approached to-her and-said my-Lord interrogative-nation even righteous kill

tokens.note: The vav is contrastive: 'but'.
qatal of קָרַב with לֹא: a completed negative act in the past.
wayyiqtol after the qatal of the previous clause.
אֲדֹנָי with qamats, addressing God in the dream (decisions, 18:3). The pack has no Ibn Ezra comment on this word; see apparatus.
The interrogative he is prefixed. Ibn Ezra reads 'the nation', the people under the king.
yiqtol 2ms of הָרַג with God as the subject: 'kill in judgment' (Qal 2).

phrases.english: But Abimelech had not approached her
phrases.literal: and-Abimelech not approached to-her: the vav is contrast

phrases.english: Will you kill a nation, even a righteous one
phrases.literal: interrogative-nation even righteous kill: the question word stands with the noun, the concessive 'even' before the adjective

grammar: The qatal לֹא קָרַב, in a clause that begins with the subject (וַאֲבִימֶלֶךְ), states the circumstance: he had not come near her. The wayyiqtol וַיֹּאמַר then takes up the narrative.
The interrogative הֲ on גּוֹי makes the whole speech a question; גַּם צַדִּיק is concessive, 'even a righteous one'.
The etnaḥta on אֵלֶיהָ divides the verse into the circumstance (what he had not done) and his speech to God.
The speech is addressed to God, and the 2ms yiqtol תַּהֲרֹג has God as its subject: the English 'will you kill' keeps the addressee.
segments.note: The vav of וַאֲבִימֶלֶךְ marks contrast with the man in danger: the king had not come near her. Ibn Ezra's reading of הַגּוֹי as the nation (not 'man') decides the English 'a nation'. His motives for the king's plea are commentary.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: the sense of 'the nation, also the righteous, you would kill' is 'on behalf of his soul, his house and his kingdom' (בְּעַד נַפְשׁוֹ וּבֵיתוֹ וּמַמְלַכְתּוֹ). He takes הַגּוֹי as the nation, and tells the reader not to heed 'the dreamer' who exchanges word for word, explaining הַגּוֹי as 'man' (אִישׁ); he refers on to his note on לְעַם נָכְרִי (Exodus 21:8). The English takes 'a nation'.

Radak: 'if you kill me, it is as if my people die with me, since I am a king who leads them in justice'. He calls himself righteous, since he took her in good faith and was not guilty of a capital crime. The English 'a nation' and 'a righteous one' match this.
Targum Onkelos renders הַגּוֹי as 'the people' (הֲעָם), so 'will you kill the people, even a righteous one?' The English agrees on 'a nation'.
Sforno: is it fitting that the nation be destroyed by killing its king, and that a righteous king be killed for what he did not do? He reads גּוֹי as the people; the English follows.
Rashi: the angel held him back, as God says, 'I did not let you touch her.' The English says only that he had not approached her; who held him back is not in the words.

Rashi, in his midrash: 'even if he is righteous, will you kill him? Is it your way to destroy nations for nothing? You did so to the generation of the flood and to the generation of the Dispersion.' This is an objection, not the plain sense; it is kept because a reader may take it.
Radak: the desire was held back by God's will. This is a reason for the verb, not its sense.

apparatus: אֲדֹנָי with qamats: the pack has no Ibn Ezra comment on this word. 'My Lord' is taken as address to God, the speaker of the dream. The other reading, 'my lord' for a man, is recorded here; it would make the king address the messenger.

segments.english: Did he not himself say to me, 'She is my sister'? And she also said, 'He is my brother.' In the integrity of my heart and in the innocence of my hands I did this."
segments.literal: did-not he himself said to-me my-sister she and-she also she said my-brother he in-integrity of-my-heart and-in-innocence of-my-hands I-did this

tokens.note: הֲלֹא: an interrogative that expects yes; the question asks 'did he not say?'
The emphatic pronoun is the subject of אָמַר.
The lexicon's sense 3: integrity.
The inner man, the heart.
Freedom from guilt.
כַּפַּיִם is a dual construct: the palms of the hands.

phrases.english: Did he not himself say to me
phrases.literal: did-not he-himself say to-me: the question word is placed before the subject
and-she also she said: the second statement repeats the pronoun for emphasis

phrases.english: In the integrity of my heart
and in the innocence of my hands

grammar: The two statements are parallel: הוּא ... אֲחֹתִי הִוא and וְהִיא ... אָחִי הוּא. The pronoun opens each half, and 'sister' and 'brother' answer each other.
The clause וּבְנִקְיֹן כַּפַּי is parallel with בְּתֹם לְבָבִי: two prepositional phrases describe the single act.
The etnaḥta on הוּא ends Abimelech's quotation of the two statements; the second half of the verse is his plea. The silluq on זֹאת ends the verse.
The question הֲלֹא expects the answer yes, and so puts the weight of the argument on Abraham's own words, and Sarah's.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'also' (גַּם) includes her servants, camels and donkeys; he asked them all and they told him 'he is her brother'. The English keeps 'also' in its ordinary sense and does not name the servants.
Rashi: 'in the integrity of my heart' means 'I did not intend to sin'. The English keeps the wider word 'integrity' (lexicon sense 3).
Rashi: 'in the innocence of my hands' means 'I did not touch her'. The English keeps 'hands' as the Hebrew does.
Radak: Abimelech asked Abraham about her, since he did not rely on his servants' questions. This is a gloss on the scene, not a sense of the words.
Radak: his heart was not toward evil, and had he thought her another man's wife, his heart would not have been set on her. A gloss on the phrase, not a sense of its words.

apparatus: הִוא (20:5.6, 20:5.9): the consonants are הוא (the form of 'he'), vocalised and read as the feminine הִיא (the Pentateuch's standing qere). The English follows the qere, 'she'. In 20:5.7 the same pronoun is written with yod.

segments.english: God said to him in a dream, "I too know that in the integrity of your heart you did this, and I also held you back from sinning against me. That is why I did not let you touch her.
segments.literal: and-said to-him the-God in-dream also I knew that in-integrity of-your-heart you-did this and-I-kept-back also I you from-sinning to-me upon so not I-gave-you to-touch to-her

tokens.note: The article with the plural form: the God who speaks. The decisions give 'God' for this verse.
A dream with a message, as in 20:3.
wayyiqtol 1cs of חָשַׂךְ: 'restrain, check'. God's restraint of the king.
The object marker with the 2ms suffix: 'you'.
Infinitive construct of חָטָא with מִן: 'from sinning'.
לִי with the infinitive: 'sin against me'. Radak takes it as a sin against God's command.
עַל כֵּן, the idiom.
qatal 1cs of נָתַן with the 2ms suffix: 'I gave you (leave)'; English 'let'.
Infinitive construct with ל, which Ibn Ezra takes as a verbal noun (שֵׁם פֹּעַל).

phrases.english: God said to him in a dream

phrases.literal: also I know that: the perfect of a verb of knowing is present

phrases.english: in the integrity of your heart
and I also held you back
phrases.literal: and-held-back also I (object) you: the vav begins the clause

phrases.english: I did not let you touch her

grammar: The sequence is qatal (יָדַעְתִּי), wayyiqtol (וָאֶחְשֹׂךְ), qatal (נְתַתִּיךָ): knowledge, the restraint that followed, and the consequence in the last clause.
The infinitive לִנְגֹּעַ has the ל prefix and follows the negative qatal: 'did not let you (touch)'.
The form מֵחֲטוֹ is an infinitive construct of the lamed-alef root חטא, with a vav for the alef (Radak).
The etnaḥta on לִי divides the speech: what God knew and did; then the result, introduced by עַל־כֵּן. The silluq on אֵלֶיהָ ends the verse.
segments.note: The speaker is הָאֱלֹהִים (with the article, of the God of Israel): 'God', as is אֱלֹהִים in 20:3. נְתַתִּיךָ is 'I gave you', the idiom 'I did not let you'; Rashi's gloss 'I did not give you the power' is covered by 'let'.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: the form לִנְגֹּעַ (with the nun) and לָגַעַת (without it) are the same, as לִנְטוֹעַ (Isaiah 51:16) beside לִטַּעַת (Ecclesiastes 3:2); all are verbal nouns (שֵׁמוֹת פֹּעַל), i.e. infinitives. The English 'to touch' is the infinitive; his point concerns the form, not the sense.

Rashi: 'I did not let you' means 'it was not from you that you did not touch her; I held you back and did not give you the power' (כֹּחַ). The English 'did not let you' takes נתן in this sense of giving leave.
Rashi: 'True, you did not imagine at the first that you were sinning; but cleanness of hands is not here.' The English gives God's words 'integrity of your heart' and says nothing of the hands.

Radak: to God the sin was open, if he broke His commands. He commanded Noah's sons about a man's wife; and even without a command, reason teaches against it, for one who gave man reason has in effect commanded him against every evil, and violence against a man's wife is violence against his body (the two are one flesh). So the sin is against God: 'against me'.
Radak: the vav stands in place of the alef of the lamed-alef verb in מֵחֲטוֹ. The English reads the infinitive of 'sin' as the form requires.
Radak: לִנְגֹּעַ covers any touch short of intercourse, kissing and embracing included, so God kept the king from all intimacy. The English 'touch' keeps this breadth.
Targum Onkelos: 'I also withheld you from sinning before me' (קָדָמַי, in my sight). The English 'against me' keeps the Hebrew dative; Onkelos's 'before me' is a near reading.
Radak: the text does not say 'cleanness of hands', because the heart is known only to God. A reason for the wording, not a sense of the words.
Radak: God held the king back from desire, and this was a kindness done in this way. A reason for the 'therefore', not a sense of the words.

apparatus: Both 20:3 (אֱלֹהִים) and 20:6 (הָאֱלֹהִים) give 'God'. Ibn Ezra's reading of 20:3, that a messenger came, is recorded there.

segments.english: Now return the man's wife, for he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live. And if you do not return her, know that you will surely die, you and all that is yours."
segments.literal: and-now return wife-of the-man for prophet he and-will-pray for-you and-live and-if you-are-not returning know that surely-die you-will-die you and-all that to-you

tokens.note: The adverb 'now' introduces the command.
Imperative hifil of שׁוּב, 'cause to return': 'give back, restore' (Hiph 1.d), the object being the man's wife.
construct of אִשָּׁה: 'wife'.
yiqtol of the hitpael of פָּלַל: 'pray'.
בַּעַד: 'on your behalf'.
The Hebrew imperative after the yiqtol is a promised consequence. Radak and Sforno read 'be healed' (commentary).
אֵין with the 2ms suffix: 'you are not' (here, not returning).
Hifil participle of שׁוּב: 'giving back, restoring' (Hiph 1.d); the object 'her' is understood.
Infinitive absolute before the yiqtol: emphasis.
כָּל with the relative: 'all that belongs to you'.

לָךְ: the pack parses the suffix as 2nd person feminine singular. The vowel is the pausal form (at the silluq) of the masculine לְךָ; Abimelech is addressed throughout, so the English 'yours' is masculine. The pack's data is kept.

phrases.english: and he will pray for you
And if you do not return her
phrases.literal: and-if you-are-not returning: the object is understood as 'her'

phrases.english: you and all that is yours

grammar: The imperative הָשֵׁב and the yiqtol וְיִתְפַּלֵּל lead to the promise of the imperative וֶחְיֵה: the clause of consequence.
The clause כִּי נָבִיא הוּא gives the reason for the command: he is a prophet, and so his prayer will work.
The conditional וְאִם־אֵֽינְךָ מֵשִׁיב is an open condition; the participle מֵשִׁיב is a present or future.
The infinitive absolute מוֹת before the yiqtol תָּמוּת gives emphasis: 'you will surely die'. The etnaḥta on וֶֽחְיֵ֑ה ends the first part.

commentary.summary: Targum Onkelos renders the command as 'return the man's wife' (אֲתֵיב אִתַּת גַּבְרָא). The English agrees.
Radak: God will not forgive until the prophet prays, so Abimelech must make his peace with Abraham even though he sinned in good faith. A reason for the prayer, not a sense of the words.
Radak: וֶחְיֵה means 'be healed' (וְתֵרָפֵא), as in 'until they were healed' (Joshua 5:8) and 'he recovered' (Isaiah 38:21). The English 'you will live' keeps the basic sense.
Sforno: 'now' means before you are consumed by the illness. The English gives 'now' and says nothing of the illness.
Sforno: 'live' means 'be healed', as in 'until they were healed' (Joshua 5:8). The English keeps 'live'.
Sforno: 'all that is yours' means the children in the wombs of your wife and of your maidservants. The English keeps the general phrase.

context: נָבִיא 'prophet': this is the first use of the word in the Bible, and it is said of Abraham. The lexicon glosses it 'spokesman, speaker'. In this verse the weight falls on his prayer (a hithpael of פלל, 'pray, intercede'), not on a message. Prophets who spoke in the name of a god are also attested at Mari, in the eighteenth century BCE.

segments.english: Abimelech rose early in the morning and summoned all his servants and spoke all these words in their hearing, and the men were greatly afraid.

phrases.english: and the men were greatly afraid

grammar: The wayyiqtol forms (וַיַּשְׁכֵּם, וַיִּקְרָא, וַיְדַבֵּר, וַיִּירְאוּ) continue the story; the change of subject is at the verb for the men.
The etnaḥta on בְּאָזְנֵיהֶם divides the verse: the king's acts, then the effect on the men. The silluq on מְאֹד ends the verse, with the adverb as the last word.
The verb וַיַּשְׁכֵּם, hifil of שָׁכַם, is the idiom 'to rise early', which the English keeps.
The noun phrase הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה has the article on both noun and demonstrative, as Hebrew requires when a demonstrative follows a definite noun.
segments.note: The idiom 'in their ears' (בְּאׇזְנֵיהֶם) is rendered 'in their hearing', which keeps the idiom. Radak's identification of the men as the servants who had praised Sarah is kept in the commentary.

commentary.summary: Radak: the men are the servants who had agreed to take the woman and had praised her to the king so that he would take her. The English keeps the general word 'the men'.
Radak: Abimelech rose early because his heart was anxious about the dream, and he would not wait for the kings to wake. A gloss on the reason, not a sense of the words.

context: עֲבָדָיו 'his servants': in royal usage עֶבֶד is the word for a king's officials, the members of his court, not only for slaves.
